item.title: Modeling capacitor voltage in an RC circuit from data: Construction, breakdown, and revision of an empirical model
item.description: arXiv:2609.08792v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We describe a guided introductory laboratory activity in which students construct empirical models of capacitor voltage in RC circuits from measured input-output data before circuit theory is introduced. Students may use what they know about resistors, Ohm's law, and conservation of charge and energy, but prior knowledge of capacitor behavior is not used as a reason for adopting a model. The circuits use a 1.5-V battery, resistors, and electric double-layer capacitors with nominal capacitances of 4.7 and 10 F. Their slow responses are recorded with handheld voltmeters and smartphone video, and the capacitance values are presented to students with the unit withheld. To compare circuits, students rescale time by the product of the nominal resistance and capacitance, as proposed by the instructor. On this coordinate, plots of the logarithm of the normalized discharging voltage are approximately straight lines through the origin, providing empirical models. For charging, the corresponding logarithmic plots are clearly curved, and the discharging model breaks down. Using the remaining distance from the final value as the dependent variable gives approximately straight logarithmic plots and provides a basis for revising the model. Rewriting the discharging model in equivalent differential and integral forms allows students to compare changes in charge-like and energy-like quantities with the charge transferred through the resistor and the energy dissipated in it. Standard circuit theory, introduced afterward, describes charging and discharging in a common form and gives these quantities their conventional meanings.
item.dc:creator: Kazumasa Kushida

item.title: R{\o}mer all ears: An auditory analog of Ole R{\o}mer's demonstration of the finite speed of light using smartphones as an acoustic vernier
item.description: arXiv:2611.31698v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present an undergraduate experiment for teaching Ole Roemer's 1676 method for demonstrating the finite speed of light. Two smartphones emit periodic sound pulses whose synchronization is evaluated directly by the observer's hearing, acting as an "acoustic vernier" that achieves millisecond travel-time resolution without microphones or external sensors. Because the measurement relies strictly on propagation delays between stationary stations, it establishes a direct experimental analogy to Roemer's original argument and dispenses with auxiliary wave phenomena absent from the 1676 analysis, such as acoustic beats or the Doppler effect. The pedagogical strength of the experiment lies precisely in this direct appeal to the senses. Loss of synchronization becomes perceptible starting at a separation of approximately 5 m and grows progressively clearer across several tens of meters. Despite its simplicity, systematic blind measurements determine the speed of sound in air with single-run uncertainties of 2 to 5 m/s (around 1%) and agree within 1.1% with theoretical predictions across ambient temperatures from 9 to 25 $^\circ$C. Beyond numerical measurement, anchoring the method in explicit sensory perception helps to clarify the recurring conceptual entanglement between Roemer's geometric delay and the kinematic Doppler effect, while highlighting how this same travel-time principle underpins contemporary astrophysical techniques, such as pulsar timing and eclipse timing variations (ETV).
item.dc:creator: La\'is Florencio de Oliveira, Gabriel Antonio Carit\'a, Jo\~ao Teles de Carvalho-Neto
